title: Introduction to Electromobility — Explainer
examSource: Built from lectures F1 (introduction), F2 (charging infrastructure), F3 (smart charging and V2X), F4 (electric vehicles and vehicle dynamics), F5 (electrical machines) and F7 (batteries for electromobility), 2026; the e-exam is on 8 January 2027.

steps.text: Electromobility means using electric powertrains, connected vehicles and charging infrastructure to move people and goods. It covers battery electric vehicles, plug-in hybrids and hydrogen fuel cell vehicles, and reaches from e-bikes to buses, ships and aircraft.

It is much more than the vehicle. Electromobility ties together electric powertrains, motors, power electronics and batteries; the charging infrastructure and how long charging takes; the environment; and the economics of purchase, charging and maintenance. Politics steers it all through regulation and funding.

In this course you learn the types of electric vehicles and their pros and cons, the components of the driveline, scenarios for society and sustainability, and what charging demands from the electric grid. The written e-exam is worth 70 points, and the seminars and group project add bonus points on top.

chapters.title: A Brief History of Electric Cars

steps.text: Electric cars are older than you might think. An electric tricycle drove in Paris in 1881, the first practical electric car followed in 1888, and by 1890 a six-passenger electric car reached 22.5 km/h. Electric trams and trolleybuses filled the cities.
In the 1920s the interest collapsed. Large oil discoveries made petrol cheap, better roads meant people drove farther, and combustion cars had the range that electric ones lacked.

From the late 1960s, rising oil prices, petrol shortages and air pollution brought electric drive back. In 1971 an electric rover drove on the Moon during Apollo 15. California pushed for zero-emission vehicles, the Toyota Prius made hybrids mainstream, the Tesla Roadster showed a 322 km range, and the Nissan Leaf brought the electric car to the mass market.

Today lithium-ion pack prices have fallen to about $108/kWh, and electrification has reached heavy transport. The Volvo FH Aero Electric truck targets 600 km of range, and the Megawatt Charging System delivers up to 1.44 MW, about 40 minutes from 20 to 80%.

On water, Stockholm's Candela P-12 electric hydrofoil cut the Ekerö commute from 55 to 30 minutes, with 66% less energy and 94% less CO₂. Autonomous ferries, shuttles and robotaxis already carry passengers, and electric aircraft such as the 30-seat Heart Aerospace ES-30 aim to enter service in the 2030s.

The European Green Deal aims for net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, with a cut of at least 55% by 2030 compared with 1990. By 2024 EU emissions were 39.5% below the 1990 level, so the hardest part is still ahead.

In 2021 the Fit for 55 package turned the targets into law. From 2035, new cars and vans with a combustion engine can no longer be placed on the EU market. The alternative fuels infrastructure rules force charging and refuelling to be built along roads and in ports, and ReFuelEU Aviation pushes sustainable aviation fuel.

Sweden goes further: domestic transport emissions 70% lower by 2030 than in 2010, net-zero by 2045, and negative emissions after that. EU road transport emissions may have peaked in 2025, and public charging points passed 1.1 million, but further cuts are still needed.

Charging comes in three levels. Level 1 is slow AC from a household socket, 1 to 2 kW, eight to twenty hours to 80%. Level 2 is AC from a wallbox or public post, 7 to 22 kW, three to eight hours. DC fast charging delivers 50 to 350 kW or more and takes a car from 0 to 80% in 15 to 45 minutes.

The key difference is where AC becomes DC. With AC charging, the converter is the on-board charger inside the car, and its rating, often 11 kW, limits the speed. With DC charging, the conversion happens in the station, which can be far bigger, so the power is limited by the station and the battery instead.

Connectors follow the same split. Type 1 is single-phase AC, used in North America and Japan. Type 2, the Mennekes plug, takes single- and three-phase AC and is the EU standard. CCS adds two DC pins below the AC plug and is the global fast-charging standard. CHAdeMO, the early DC standard of the Nissan Leaf, is being phased out, and GB/T is China's standard for both AC and DC.

Sweden, with about 10.6 million people, has seen chargeable cars grow steeply since 2013, and Uppsala alone has more than 300 public charging points. Most charging, though, still happens at home and at work.

Beyond the cable, there are three families. Static charging while parked, either conductive through a plug or wireless. Dynamic charging while driving, on an electric road system. And battery swapping, where the empty battery is exchanged for a full one.

Inductive charging uses a magnetic field between a coil in the ground and a coil under the car, like a phone on a charging pad, at about 85 to 90% efficiency. It works parked or, with coils in the road, while driving. Capacitive charging uses an electric field between plates instead: potentially lighter, but still experimental.

Electric road systems feed vehicles while they drive: through overhead lines like a trolleybus, a conductive rail in the road, or inductive coils beneath it. Sweden has trialled all three, with overhead lines at Sandviken, rails at Arlanda and Lund, and coils in Visby. But the first permanent electric road, on the E20 between Hallsberg and Örebro, was removed from the national plan in 2025 because of cost.

Battery swapping replaces the battery instead of recharging it, in about 3 to 5 minutes, as in Nio's swap stations. It suits taxis and fleets, but it needs standardised battery packs across vehicles, which carmakers rarely agree on.

Compared side by side: static plug-in charging is cheap at home and scales well, but you have to plug in. Dynamic charging charges continuously but is very expensive to build. Wireless charging is hands-free but slower. Swapping is the fastest, but only works for fleets with a common battery.

Charging can be automated too. At level 0 a human plugs in the cable. Levels 1 to 3 add increasing assistance. At level 4 the car positions itself and a robot arm connects the plug. At level 5 charging needs no human at all, which is what a robotaxi needs.

When should you charge? The spot price of electricity changes every hour: low at night and when wind and sun are plentiful, high at the morning and evening peaks. Smart charging moves the charging to cheap hours, which saves money and eases the load on the grid.

Trucks need far more power. A long-haul truck battery holds several hundred kilowatt hours, so depots and freight corridors need megawatt chargers, and Sweden's first public MCS demonstration took place at the Milence hub in Landvetter. Charging has to fit into the driver's mandatory rest breaks.

Looking ahead, Swedish airports aim to be fossil-free by 2050, with electrified ground operations, renewable energy, storage and the airport as a regional energy hub. Solar-powered tractors and drones show that electric propulsion reaches everywhere. The open question for a national charging plan: coverage, speed, or cost first?

The electrical grid was built for one-way flow: large power plants, transmission lines, then distribution to homes. Now it is turning two-way, with solar on rooftops, wind farms, batteries and local microgrids. Electric vehicles arrive in the middle of this change as a large new load.

Left alone, most people plug in when they get home, so charging piles onto the evening peak around six to eight o'clock, exactly when households already use the most. With many EVs, that means higher peaks, voltage drops and overloaded transformers and lines. But the same cars are parked most of the day, so they could also be part of the solution.

There are four charging strategies. The first is uncontrolled, or dumb, charging. The car is treated as an ordinary load: charging starts the moment it is plugged in and runs until the battery is full. The price is assumed constant, nothing nudges the user to wait, and the only cure for the extra peak is expensive grid reinforcement.

The second is multiple tariff charging, or time-of-use pricing. Electricity is cheaper in off-peak valley hours, so owners are encouraged to charge then, but they still decide. It shifts part of the demand, yet it is still counted as uncontrolled, and if thousands of EVs all start when the cheap tariff begins, they create a new peak of their own.

The third is smart, or controlled, charging. An aggregator, or the distribution system operator in an isolated system, manages the charging power of many cars at once. It schedules charging around grid conditions, market prices and available generation, while still delivering what each user needs. This prevents overloads and voltage problems, avoids costly reinforcements, and lets the fleet sell ancillary services by adjusting how fast it charges.

The fourth is bidirectional charging, called V2G or more generally V2X. Now the aggregator controls both charging and discharging, so the cars become distributed energy storage that can push power back during high demand. It offers more reserve than smart charging alone, for peak shaving, load balancing and voltage support. The cost is extra battery cycling and degradation, so owners need a bigger financial incentive.

Side by side: dumb charging gives the user full control, no grid control and very limited benefit. Multiple tariff keeps user control and adds price signals, for a moderate benefit. Smart charging hands control to the aggregator or DSO, with high benefit. Only vehicle-to-grid also exports power back to the grid.

V2X comes in several forms. V2L, vehicle-to-load, powers a device directly, for camping, an outage or a rural site. V2H, vehicle-to-home, runs the house during expensive hours or a blackout. V2B does the same for commercial and industrial buildings, with larger benefits. And V2G, vehicle-to-grid, sells one or more energy services to the grid itself. Smart charging without export is often called V1G.

chapters.title: What EV Flexibility Offers the Grid

steps.text: The first opportunity is reshaping the load curve. Smart V1G charging fills the night-time valley, when power is cheap and plentiful. V2G goes further and shaves the evening peak by feeding power back, so fewer expensive fossil peak plants need to run.

The second is ancillary services for the transmission grid. Grid frequency must stay close to 50 Hz in Europe. An aggregated EV fleet can respond within 500 ms, faster than thermal power plants, which makes it ideal for the primary frequency reserve, FCR. V2G inverters can also inject or absorb reactive power to support the voltage.

Next come the local problems. When a line is congested, the operator can pause or slow charging in that area only, which can defer cable upgrades worth millions of euros. In residential streets, many home chargers of 11 kW running together can overload a feeder; spreading them across the night solves it. And fast chargers can support the local voltage with reactive power.

Flexible charging also soaks up renewable energy. At midday, when solar peaks, parked workplace fleets can act as green energy sponges instead of the clean power being curtailed. Behind the meter, a household charges at the cheapest night hours, runs the home from the car in the evening, and lowers the total cost of ownership.

So who benefits? Transmission operators, the TSOs, gain frequency control and peak reduction. Distribution operators, the DSOs, gain congestion relief and local voltage control. Consumers gain lower bills. What is still missing is the ecosystem: charging and grid planned together, clear roles for every actor, regulation and business models for flexibility markets, common standards, and rules for data.

All of this is demand-side flexibility: end users deliberately changing their consumption, or generation, in response to prices, market signals or the system operator. Its goals are a flatter load profile, more renewables and lower operating costs. Passenger EVs are parked up to 90% of the time, which makes them an excellent resource, as long as smart meters and communication technology track consumption, send dynamic tariffs and automate the adjustments.

V2G services differ by response time. Frequency regulation and voltage support act in milliseconds to seconds. Operating reserves act in seconds to minutes. Peak shaving, renewable integration and congestion management work over minutes to hours, valley filling over hours, and capacity markets over hours to days. Most real projects stack several of these revenue streams, a practice called value stacking.

A good exercise: sort these services into energy services, which move energy in time, like arbitrage, peak shaving and renewable integration, and ancillary services, which keep the grid stable, like frequency regulation, reserves and voltage support. Then ask yourself: if you owned an electric car, would you join V2G, and on what conditions?

Range anxiety, the fear of running out of battery before reaching your destination, has long been one of the main barriers to electric cars. As ranges grow, the question is changing from can I get there, to can I charge when I get there. Drivers now worry about finding a free charger, whether it works, how long they will wait, and what it costs.

Many things change how far a car really goes. The driver: driving style, speed and charging habits. The car: its weight, shape, tyre pressure, propulsion system and auxiliaries such as heating. And the conditions: temperature, wind, weather, road gradient, traffic and route length.

Temperature matters most of all. Range is best around 25 °C and drops sharply in the cold, when the battery is sluggish and the cabin must be heated. In a long test of a Nissan Leaf in the UK, the energy used per kilometre differed by around 70% between the cold and warm months.

chapters.title: Vehicle Dynamics: The Forces on a Car

steps.text: Range follows from simple physics. Power is force times speed. Energy is power times time. Put them together and the distance you can drive is the battery energy times the speed, divided by the power you draw. Draw more power at the same speed, and the range falls.

The motor has to supply four forces. The acceleration force to change speed, the rolling resistance of the tyres, the aerodynamic drag of the air, and the climbing force on a slope. Together they make up the motive force the drivetrain must deliver.
The acceleration force is Newton's second law: mass times acceleration. The wheels, motor and gears must spin up too, which adds roughly 5% on top.
steps.equation: F_a = m\,a = m\,\frac{dv}{dt} \qquad F_a + F_{\omega a} \approx 1.05\,F_a

steps.text: Aerodynamic drag is one half, times the air density, times the drag coefficient, times the frontal area, times the speed squared. The speed here is relative to the air, so a headwind adds to it and a tailwind subtracts. Air density depends on temperature, humidity and altitude, and the drag coefficient on how streamlined the car is.

Try it. A car with a drag coefficient of 0.25, a frontal area of 2 square metres and 20 kWh of usable energy drives at 120 km/h, about 33.3 metres per second. In calm air the drag is about 333 newtons, which takes 11.1 kW, giving a range of 216 km. A 12 km/h headwind raises the drag to 403 newtons and cuts the range to 179 km. The same tailwind stretches it to 267 km.

Rolling resistance comes from the tyres deforming on the road and from friction in the drivetrain. It is the rolling coefficient times the mass times g, 9.81 metres per second squared, and it barely depends on speed. A car of 2000 kg with a coefficient of 0.0085 feels about 167 newtons; at 10 km/h that costs only about 464 watts.

The climbing force is the mass times g times the sine of the slope angle. Uphill it adds to what the motor must deliver. Downhill it turns negative, and the motor can regenerate energy back into the battery. A car of 1645 kg rolling down a slope of 6° at 120 km/h has about 56 kW to recover.

In practice, engineers measure drag and rolling resistance together with a coast-down test: get up to speed, shift to neutral, and record how fast the car slows. The result is the road-load force, A plus B times speed plus C times speed squared. A is mainly rolling resistance, B is small rotational losses, and C is aerodynamic drag.

This explains why highway speed eats range. Rolling power grows in step with speed, but drag power grows with the cube of speed. For a Tesla Model 3, air resistance dominates at highway speeds, and even a gentle 1° incline adds a large climbing term.

Auxiliaries count too. A car with a battery of 24 kWh covers 170 km at a steady 88 km/h, so it drives for about 1.93 hours and draws about 12.4 kW. Switch on heating or air conditioning drawing 6 kW, and the total becomes about 18.4 kW. The battery now lasts only 1.3 hours, and the range drops to about 114 km.

A harder one. A car of 1645 kg drives at 126 km/h, or 35 metres per second, with a road load of A equals 130, B equals 0.71 and C equals 0.49. The road load is about 755 newtons, or 26.4 kW. The battery draws 85 kW at 92% drivetrain efficiency, so 78.2 kW reaches the wheels. The extra 51.8 kW must be climbing, which gives a grade of about 5.3°, uphill.

Every electric propulsion system, in a car or a ship, has the same parts. Energy storage, usually a battery, feeds power electronics, the inverter, which drives the electric motor. A controller, fed by sensors and communication links, decides what the power electronics do. Power flows one way through the chain, information flows around it.

Vehicle types range from conventional to fully electric. A conventional car has only a combustion engine running on fuel. A hybrid, HEV, uses the engine as primary and an electric motor as secondary, still filled only with fuel. A plug-in hybrid, PHEV, flips this, with the electric motor as primary and the engine as backup, using both fuel and electricity. A battery electric vehicle, BEV, runs on electricity alone.

Electric motors are everywhere. In 2023 motor systems used 53% of the world's electricity, about 13,462 TWh. They take 72% of industry's electricity, 87% of agriculture's, 86% of transport's and 36% of buildings'. In 2011 the estimate was about 45%, so the share is growing.

A machine needs only three cause-and-effect pairs. Ampère: a current makes a magnetic field, and a coil of N turns adds up to N times I ampere-turns. Faraday: a changing flux induces a voltage, which gives back-EMF and eddy currents, and Lenz says the induced current opposes the change. Lorentz: a current in a field feels a force, and that force at a radius is torque.

The magnetic core multiplies the field. Electrical steel has a relative permeability in the thousands, while air has about 1. So steel carries the flux around a closed magnetic circuit. The rotor must turn, so an air gap is unavoidable, and it costs many ampere-turns. Keep the gap small.

Iron is made of tiny magnetic domains. Unmagnetised, they point randomly and cancel. An applied field lines them up, until at about 1.5 to 2 tesla they are all aligned and the steel saturates. Bring the field back to zero and some flux remains, the remanence. The reverse field needed to remove it is the coercivity. The area of the loop is energy lost every cycle, the hysteresis loss.

Soft magnetic materials, like electrical steel, have a narrow loop: they magnetise easily and lose little per cycle, so they guide the flux in the stator and rotor. Hard materials, the permanent magnets NdFeB, SmCo, ferrite and AlNiCo, have a wide loop and keep their magnetisation, so they supply the rotor field without any current.

A solid steel core acts like one big shorted turn. The changing flux drives eddy currents that heat it, and the loss grows with the frequency squared and the thickness squared. The fix is thin sheets, typically 0.2 to 0.5 mm, insulated from each other. The windings are copper, the magnets supply the rotor flux, and polymer insulation with air, water or oil cooling keeps the temperature in bounds.

Feed one coil with DC and the rotor turns toward it, then stops. A single phase has dead points with no torque, and two phases work but the power is not smooth. Three currents, shifted by 120°, give three pulsating fields that add up to one field of constant size, rotating at constant speed. Three phases give constant power.

The field turns at the synchronous speed: 120 times the frequency, divided by the number of poles, in rpm. A two-pole machine at 50 Hz turns at 3000 rpm, a four-pole one at 1500 rpm. More poles means a slower field. In an EV the inverter varies the frequency, so the speed is set electronically: at 200 Hz the four-pole machine reaches 6000 rpm.

The rotor has its own field and is dragged along by the stator field, like one magnet following another. The torque is proportional to the stator field, times the rotor field, times the sine of the load angle between them. A salient iron rotor adds reluctance torque, because iron also wants to line up with the field. Distributed windings give a smoother field, concentrated windings are more compact.

Power is torque times speed. When it is positive, electrical power goes in and mechanical power comes out: the machine is a motor. When it is negative, mechanical power goes in and electrical power comes out: it is a generator, or a brake. The same hardware does both, which is how regenerative braking works in an EV, forwards and in reverse.

All AC machines share the same stator and rotating field. What differs is how the rotor gets its field. Induced currents give the induction, or asynchronous, machine. Permanent magnets give the permanent-magnet synchronous machine, PMSM. DC in a rotor winding gives the wound-field synchronous machine. Shaped iron alone gives the reluctance machine.

In an induction machine the rotor is just conductors in steel. It turns slightly slower than the field, and this slip induces rotor currents, by Faraday, which feel a force in the stator field, by Lorentz. No slip, no torque. It is robust, simple and free of magnets, with no back-EMF at a fault. But the rotor copper losses lower its efficiency and power density.

In a PMSM, magnets on the rotor lock onto the rotating field. There is no rotor current and so no rotor copper loss, which gives the highest efficiency and power density: the choice of most EVs, like the Toyota Prius and Chevrolet Volt. The catch: it makes back-EMF whenever it spins, even at a fault, and magnets bring cost, supply risk and demagnetisation limits.

A wound-field synchronous machine feeds DC into a rotor winding, through slip rings and brushes or a brushless exciter. Its field can be adjusted, or switched off at a fault. Power-station generators work this way, and so does the Renault ZOE. The price is rotor copper loss, extra parts and complexity.

Magnets trade strength for temperature and cost. NdFeB is the strongest, 1.0 to 1.4 tesla, but only up to about 80 to 200 °C, with rare-earth supply risk. SmCo, 0.8 to 1.1 tesla, survives 250 to 350 °C but is costly. Ferrite is cheap and free of rare earths, but only 0.2 to 0.45 tesla, and it demagnetises when cold. AlNiCo is very stable but easily demagnetised, and mostly legacy.

The magnets can sit on the rotor surface, which is simple but needs a retaining sleeve. Buried inside, in an interior PM machine, they add reluctance torque and a wide field-weakening range. In a spoke rotor they stand radially and concentrate the flux, so weak, cheap ferrite can reach a high air-gap flux. That is how a rare-earth-free ferrite spoke design can replace the earlier NdFeB design in the same space.

Compare them. The induction machine has significant rotor copper losses and no magnets, with good efficiency: early Teslas and industry. The PM machine has small rotor losses and the highest efficiency and power density: most EVs. The wound-field machine adjusts its flux, with field copper losses. Reluctance machines are robust but noisy, and DC machines, once dominant, lost out to power electronics.

Efficiency is the output power over the input power. Copper loss is I squared R heat in the windings. Iron loss is hysteresis and eddy currents in the steel. Mechanical loss is bearing friction and windage, and magnets add eddy-current loss. At low speed and high torque copper loss dominates; at high speed iron and magnet losses take over. So design for the drive cycle, not only the peak.

Each application wants something different from a battery. Consumer electronics want 150 to 300 Wh/kg at any cost, but only 500 to 1000 cycles and 2 to 3 years. Grid storage wants the lowest cost and 15 to 20 years, while 50 to 100 Wh/kg is enough. An EV sits in between: 100 to 150 Wh/kg, $100 to $150/kWh, −20 to 60 °C, 10 to 15 years and 3000 to 7000 cycles, with fast charge and discharge.

Batteries have driven cars from the start. In 1899 La Jamais Contente, the never contented, was the first car to pass 100 km/h. It had two motors and 50 kW, but it weighed 1450 kg, and half of that was its 100 lead-acid cells. Charging took 7 hours. Weight and range made combustion engines more appealing for the next hundred years.

The degree of electrification runs from a pure combustion car, through start-stop, mild and strong hybrids, HEV, and the plug-in hybrid, PHEV, to the full EV. An extended-range EV, EREV, drives only on its motor and uses a small engine solely to charge the battery. The right choice depends on the electric range needed, the energy use per km, the performance wanted and the climate and terrain.

A hybrid runs in charge-sustaining mode: the state of charge wobbles around a set level and the battery never empties. A plug-in hybrid first charges from the grid, runs down in charge-depleting mode, then switches to charge sustaining. An EV is charge depleting all the way. So the packs differ: under 3 kWh for an HEV, 5 to 15 kWh for a PHEV, and 30 to 100 kWh for an EV.

Usage matters too. Hybrid trucks on urban, rural and inter-city routes see very different speed profiles: frequent stops in town, a steady 80 to 90 km/h between cities. Their state of charge spends most time near the lower limit, because the hybrid strategy draws the battery down during acceleration. The same chemistry ages differently on each route.

Battery design starts from the vehicle. Its weight, rolling resistance, auxiliary loads, temperature, energy management and electric range set two numbers: the power, which fixes the C-rate, and the energy, which fixes the capacity. Together they select the battery technology. Four general criteria follow: mechanical stability, temperature, battery life and voltage characteristics.

A pack joins hundreds of cells, so it must be mechanically stable from cell to pack. The connections between cells must carry current with little leakage and withstand vibration, corrosion must be avoided, and in a crash the pack's encapsulation and its place in the vehicle must protect the cells.

Temperature sets the limits for performance, safety and life. Specifications run from −40 to 80 °C, but cycle life falls fast when the cell is hot: at 60 °C it fades far sooner than at 25 °C. Cells make Joule heat, I squared R, so packs need cooling. Air cooling is cheap with no risk of leaks, but too weak for fast charging; liquid cooling performs better but costs more. In the cold, a heater is needed, because charging a cold cell can grow lithium dendrites.

A battery reaches end of life at 80% of its beginning-of-life capacity, though it still works below that. Calendar life counts years, cycle life counts charge and discharge cycles, and shelf life is storage without use. The state of charge is the share of capacity still available, the depth of discharge the share already used, and together they make 100%. The state of health, a rough estimate from capacity loss, is hard to measure.

Most devices like a flat discharge curve, so the voltage stays steady over a wide range of charge, as with LFP. But in an EV the state of charge drives energy management and the range estimate, and a flat curve hides it. A sloping curve, or one with clear voltage steps, makes the state of charge easier to read.

The battery management system is the brain of an EV. It measures voltage, current and temperature, estimates the state of charge, state of power and state of health, balances the cells, controls the thermal management, and reports to the car and the cloud.

Cells come in three formats. Cylindrical cells are cheap and mass produced, but their steel or aluminium cans are bulky: e-bikes, power tools and Tesla cars. Prismatic cells pack efficiently with higher energy density but come in many sizes: EVs and storage. Pouch cells are light and flexible with the highest energy density, but cost more and are hard to scale: phones and drones.

Cells form modules, and modules, with protection systems, form the pack. Cells in series add their voltage; strings in parallel add their capacity. 8S2P means 8 cells in series and 2 such strings in parallel, 16 cells. With cells of 3.6 V and 5 Ah that gives 28.8 V and 10 Ah. A 16S4P module has twice the voltage and twice the capacity.

Tesla's cells grew from the 18650, 18 mm by 65 mm, to the 2170 and the 4680, 46 mm by 80 mm. Bigger cells mean fewer cells and welds, easier management, more active material, higher energy density and a lower cost per Wh.

Cell energy is capacity times voltage. Today's electrodes are intercalation hosts: graphite at 372 mAh/g and 0.15 V versus lithium, or LTO at 160 mAh/g and 1.55 V, against oxide or phosphate cathodes at about 150 mAh/g and 3.7 V. Conversion electrodes promise far more: silicon at 3580 mAh/g, sulphur at 1672 mAh/g, oxygen at 3840 mAh/g. Intercalation gives excellent reversibility, conversion gives high energy.

The EV workhorses are NCM and LFP. NCM, nickel manganese cobalt oxide, has high specific energy at low cost. LFP, lithium iron phosphate, has lower energy but high power, safety and lifespan. LCO has high energy but poor safety and life. NCA has high energy but low safety. LTO is safe and long-lived but low in energy and costly.

Solid electrolytes promise safety, since they do not burn, and could enable lithium metal anodes and high-voltage cathodes. But lithium metal grows dendrites, the electrolytes are unstable at low and high voltage, ceramics are hard to manufacture, many need a dry room, and the price is high. Solid-state batteries are unlikely in EVs before 2030.

How far is electric flight? A Dornier 228 carries 1900 kg of fuel, about 22,944 kWh. At 30% turboprop efficiency that is roughly 6900 kWh of useful work. The same 1900 kg of the best battery packs, at 255 Wh/kg, holds only 484 kWh, or about 390 kWh at 80% electric efficiency. That is about 18 times less, so batteries still have a long way to go.

To recap: electromobility is vehicles, charging and policy together. AC charging is limited by the on-board charger and DC by the station. Smart charging and V2G turn parked cars into flexibility for the grid. Range comes down to physics: drag grows with the square of speed, and downhill the motor gives energy back. Motors turn a rotating field into torque, most EVs with permanent magnets. And the battery is chosen for the vehicle: power and energy, temperature, life and chemistry, with NCM and LFP leading.
